item.title: Hey, Home Slice: A la Mode Pies is coming home to PhinneyWood
item.dc:creator: Chris Maykut
item.description: After three long years away, A la Mode Pies is officially on its way back to PhinneyWood. Construction is underway on their new flagship café located on the ground floor of the […]
item.content:encoded:
After three long years away, A la Mode Pies is officially on its way back to PhinneyWood. Construction is underway on their new flagship café located on the ground floor of the new Woodland View Apartments at 59th and Phinney Ave—the exact spot where the beloved pie shop opened in 2011.

The return is a long time coming. Homestead Community Land Trust redeveloped the former property into permanent affordable housing, which meant A la Mode had to close their original Phinney location. However, owner Chris Porter, aka the Pie Guy, started planning the café’s return two years before it served its last slice in August 2023.

 “My dream of owning the best pie shop in Seattle was baked on that corner,” says Porter. “For more than a decade, Phinney embraced my big idea and made A la Mode part of this neighborhood’s story. This reopening is only happening because of that love, and now it’s my turn to give it back. I just want to bring the smell of fresh apple pie home to a neighborhood I adore.”  

The return to PhinneyWood took longer than originally hoped. Seattle’s lengthy permitting process, combined with a few unexpected hiccups, pushed the anticipated opening from this November to January 2027. Despite the delay, the Pie Guy plans to sell his handmade pies on the location’s corner during Thanksgiving week, even though the cafe won’t be open for regular business. Customers can pre-order from the Thanksgiving menu starting October 1 by visiting the A la Mode Pies website. 

“This year, our holiday pie sales are doing double duty,” says Porter, who’s funding the new café out of his own pocket. “Every pie ordered helps cover the real cost of bringing this space back to life. If you’ve ever loved a slice from A la Mode, now’s the time to order your Thanksgiving pie and help us make this our biggest turnout yet.”

In the coming months, Porter promises to share plenty of tasty tidbits exclusively with the PNA’s PhinenyWood blog. Soon, Porter will take us on a private tour inside the new space, sharing with the neighborhood an early taste of the café’s innovative design and revamped menu. We’ll also be the first to announce the grand opening date here on the blog.

Pie Meets Pint at Flying Bike

In the meantime, for those wanting to get their pie fix in now, A la Mode has teamed up with neighborhood favorite Flying Bike Cooperative Brewery to host two Thanksgiving pie-and-beer tasting events on October 17, inside the brewery’s Aviator Alcove. The back-to-back events will give A la Mode fans the first bite of four new pie additions to this year’s Thanksgiving menu, all expertly paired with Flying Bike beers.

The first tasting runs from 5–6:30 p.m., followed by a second session from 7–8:30 p.m. With only 16 seats per tasting, tickets will sell out quickly, so reserve your spot today! Ticket price: $50

Save a Slice for the Bears

A la Mode has also found a distinctly PhinneyWood way to mark its return: with pie, the Woodland Park Zoo, and a few grizzly critics. During the month of September, a portion of sales from their new Wild BEARy pie benefits the Zoo’s two resident brown bears, Fern and Juniper, by providing support for their long-term care and nourishment. A la Mode created a playful video to promote the partnership—which Porter describes as one of the most rewarding collaborations the pie shop has ever put its claws into.

So while January may feel a long way off, A la Mode is already finding creative and generous ways to reconnect with the neighborhood that established it as a Seattle dessert destination. Stay tuned for more as the cafe takes shape.

The Neighborhood Smells Better Already – Welcome Back, A la Mode Pies!

item.title: Did You Know Phinney Ridge Lutheran Church Has a Food Pantry?
item.dc:creator: Chris Maykut
item.description: There’s a neighborhood resource hiding in plain sight that many longtime PhinneyWood residents may not know about. Phinney Ridge Lutheran Church operates a community food pantry twice a week, offering […]
item.content:encoded:
There’s a neighborhood resource hiding in plain sight that many longtime PhinneyWood residents may not know about. Phinney Ridge Lutheran Church operates a community food pantry twice a week, offering groceries to neighbors who need them, with very few hoops to jump through. No appointment needed, no eligibility restrictions, and identification is not required.

The pantry is open Tuesdays from 1:15–3pm and Wednesdays from 6–8pm. The entrance is located off N 76th Street, just east of Greenwood Avenue N, at Phinney Ridge Lutheran Church. Visitors can come to the pantry up to twice each month.

The pantry keeps things simple, collecting only a visitor’s self-reported name, household size, and ZIP code. That straightforward approach is intentional: if you or your family could use some extra help putting food on the table, the pantry is there for you.

As the holidays approach, we’ll share more about the pantry’s Thanksgiving and holiday food baskets, along with ways the PhinneyWood community can help support this neighborhood resource.

Know someone who could use this resource?

Please share this information! Food insecurity doesn’t always look the way people expect it to, and needing some help with groceries doesn’t require an explanation or a particular set of circumstances.

Phinney Ridge Lutheran Church Food Pantry
7500 Greenwood Ave N., Seattle, WA 98103. Entrance on N 76th Street, just east of Greenwood Ave N.

Tuesdays: 1:15–3pm
Wednesdays: 6–8pm

Want to donate?

Food donations can be brought to the food bank during distribution hours, or to the church office during open hours (M-F, 9am – 3pm). All non-perishables are appreciated. Below are a list of items always in need:

Food Items:

  • Peanut Butter 
  • Canned Fruit 
  • Canned Vegetables 
  • Canned Soups 
  • Dry Flavored Ramen 
  • Chili or Pork and Beans 
  • Spaghetti Sauce  
  • Dried Spaghetti Noodles 
  • Boxed Mac and Cheese 
  • Rolled Oats 
  • Low-Sugar Cereals 
  • Milk, shelf-stable or powdered/dry
  • Soda Crackers 
  • Ground Coffee or Teabags 

Non-Food items:

  • Toilet Paper 
  • Deodorant 
  • Toothpaste
  • Tooth Brush
  • Shaving cream 
  • Hairbrush 
  • Comb 
  • Shampoo 
  • Dish Soap 
  • Sponges

item.title: September PhinneyWood Housing Market Snapshot
item.dc:creator: Guest Writer
item.description: This is a monthly contribution to the PhinneyWood Blog by Greenwood realtor, Doron Weisbarth. August’s PhinneyWood real estate numbers were a mixed bag. Unlike the broader King County market where […]
item.content:encoded:
This is a monthly contribution to the PhinneyWood Blog by Greenwood realtor, Doron Weisbarth.

August’s PhinneyWood real estate numbers were a mixed bag. Unlike the broader King County market where new listings finally declined, new listings here continued to increase, pushing available inventory even higher. At the same time, buyer activity picked up, with more homes going under contract than in July. However, that wasn’t enough to keep pace with the growing supply; inventory continued moving toward a more balanced market, homes took longer to sell, and prices showed signs of softening.

So, what does it all mean? Buyers are still buying, but they have more choices and sellers face more competition. Whether this is the beginning of a more balanced PhinneyWood market or simply another unusual month remains to be seen. You can find all the latest data and the full analysis online at PhinneyWoodHomes.com.

If you have questions about what’s happening in the PhinneyWood housing market or what it might mean for your home, call Doron at 206-779-9808 for a no-obligation consultation and a smart strategy tailored to your goals.

item.title: A Fresh Look Without a Full Renovation
item.dc:creator: Guest Writer
item.description: Sponsored post by Phinney Ridge Painting & Home Services Sometimes, the best way to improve your home is to take a fresh look at what’s already there. A kitchen that […]
item.content:encoded:
Sponsored post by Phinney Ridge Painting & Home Services

Sometimes, the best way to improve your home is to take a fresh look at what’s already there. A kitchen that feels dated may have well-built cabinets hiding beneath a worn finish. A living room that feels dark may benefit more from a thoughtful color palette than a major remodel. And tired trim, scuffed walls, or unfinished details can make an otherwise comfortable home feel overdue for attention. For homeowners in Phinney Ridge and surrounding core Seattle neighborhoods, interior painting and targeted carpentry offer a practical way to stretch a home improvement budget—without taking on months of construction and the coordination of multiple trades.

Keep What Works. Update What Doesn’t.

The most cost-effective improvements often begin with a simple question: What can we improve rather than replace? Cabinets are a great example. If your existing cabinets are sturdy, function well, and fit your needs, repainting or refinishing them can dramatically change the feel of a kitchen without a full replacement. Updated hardware can help complete the transformation. The key is assessing the cabinets first and choosing the right preparation and finish for their condition and material. A lasting result takes more than applying a new color.

That same approach works throughout the house. Freshly painted walls and ceilings, repaired or updated trim, and a few carefully chosen carpentry improvements such as front entry built-ins or a new custom mantle piece can make rooms feel more finished and connected. A coordinated plan helps your budget go toward changes you’ll notice and enjoy every day.

Make the Season Work for Your Budget

Fall and winter are worth considering for interior projects. As exterior painting slows down, the quieter season can bring more scheduling flexibility and opportunities for labor discounts. Ask about seasonal pricing and openings when you begin planning. If you have flexibility on your project dates, mention it. Scheduling work during a less-requested week may help your improvement dollars go further. A focused scope also helps: deciding which rooms, surfaces, and details matter most allows you to invest where the improvement will have the greatest impact.

Plan Around the Holidays—Before the Calendar Fills

The weeks leading up to and following the holidays can be useful windows for interior work, but they require advance planning. If you’re hosting Thanksgiving dinner or welcoming overnight guests in December, work backward from the date your home needs to be ready. Allow time for choosing colors, completing preparation and repairs, and giving finishes the drying or curing time they need before normal use. If your holiday calendar is already full, consider reserving a project for after the celebrations. January and February can be a welcome opportunity to refresh your home once the decorations come down.

The important step is sharing your event dates and household needs early so the work can be planned around them.

One Team, a Thoughtful Plan

You don’t have to change everything to make your home feel better. At Phinney Ridge Painting, we aim to be your trusted, one-stop shop for interior painting and carpentry—from refreshing walls and trim to updating cabinets and taking care of the details that bring a room together. We offer free in-house color consultations with a slate of independent local designers for you to choose from.

Contact Phinney Ridge Painting to plan your interior refresh, ask about fall and winter savings, and reserve dates that work around your holidays. Let’s make the most of the home you already love.

item.title: How Do You Know If You’re Lifting Heavy Enough?
item.dc:creator: Guest Writer
item.description: This is part of an ongoing series from PhinneyWood’s own Seattle Strength & Performance Strength training is becoming increasingly popular and the importance of “lifting heavy” for bone density and […]
item.content:encoded:
This is part of an ongoing series from PhinneyWood’s own Seattle Strength & Performance

Strength training is becoming increasingly popular and the importance of “lifting heavy” for bone density and muscle loss with aging is heavily discussed topic. But how heavy is “heavy” enough to get those results? There’s a lot of space between “too easy” and “too heavy,” and finding that sweet spot is one of the most important skills you can develop as a strength trainer. Don’t fret — we’re here to help! But first, a few disclaimers before we get into it:

  1. If you’re lifting any weights at all with the intention of lifting heavy – you’re doing great! Something is always better than nothing.
  2. The only “non-negotiable” here is that you participate in progressive overload by doing slightly more over time. If you’re brand new to lifting weights, you probably don’t need to stress too much about if the weights are heavy enough, you just need to go lift them.
  3. Too heavy too soon can also be an issue as it increases your risk for injury. The goal of this blog post is to help you figure out a starting point, but if your weights are increasing (even slowly) over time, you’re doing great! Keep going!

Here are three practical ways to figure out if the weight you’re using is actually heavy enough.

1. Ask Yourself How Many More Reps You Could Have Done (or literally try it!)

This is the simplest gut-check there is, and it’s more revealing than most people realize. This strategy is called “Reps in Reserve” or RIR and it’s a scale of 1-10 that many coaches use to assign intensity or difficulty to exercises. To determine your RIR, at the end of your last set, pause and ask yourself honestly: “If I absolutely had to, how many more reps could I have done with good form?” Not sloppy, grinding reps — clean ones. 

Or even better – next time you’re in the gym, try it out! Especially for exercises that don’t pose a big safety risk of failing (think dumbbell exercises, machines, etc.). Our guess? You’re way stronger than you think! If your answer (or result) is five or more, the weight is probably too light. If your answer is zero, depending on your training age, the weight might be too heavy! Training to failure is a good tool for certain goals, but probably not important or worth the potential risk in the first 6 months of strength training. 

A good general target is finishing your last set feeling like you had about two to three reps left in the tank. You’re not completely spent, but you couldn’t have gone much further without your form breaking down. That zone, where you could’ve done a few more but wouldn’t want to, is where you want to spend most of your training time.

Reps in Reserve is a useful mental model because it shifts the focus from the number on the weight to the actual demand being placed on your individual body. Two people can lift the same dumbbell and have completely different experiences depending on their strength level. What matters isn’t the specific number: it’s how challenging it is for you.

2. Watch the Speed of the Weight

A second option is to watch the speed of your reps, which can tell you a lot about whether the weight is in the right range.

Here’s the general pattern: if the weight moves very quickly and easily through the full range of motion and the last rep looks just as easy as the first one, the weight is probably too light. If it slows down toward the end of your set but you’re still able to complete the reps with good form, you’re in a good spot. If the weight grinds to a near stop and your form starts to fall apart, it’s likely too heavy for that rep range.

A practical way to use this: on your first rep of a set, notice how fast the weight moves. Now compare that to your last rep. Some slowdown is normal and expected — that’s fatigue doing its job. But if your last rep moved at about the same speed as your first, the weight probably isn’t heavy enough to create the kind of demand that builds strength over time.

On the flip side, if the weight starts moving slowly from rep one and your form is breaking down early in the set, scale back. Grinding through poor reps with a weight that’s too heavy isn’t getting you to your goals quicker, it’s likely just more risky.

3. Rate It on a Scale of 1 to 10

This one is called RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion)  and it’s a very useful tool in strength training once you get the hang of it, although it does take some time to get used to.

The concept is straightforward. After a set, you rate how hard it felt on a scale of 1 to 10. A 1 would be barely any effort at all and a 10 would be absolute maximum effort, nothing left, couldn’t do another rep if your life depended on it. RPE is also the inverse of RIR which we talked about earlier. An RPE of 10 is a RIR of 0, make sense?

For most strength training purposes, you want to be working in the 7 to 8 range on your working sets. A 7 means it was challenging but you had a few reps left. An 8 means it was hard and you had maybe two reps left. A 10 is true failure which can be useful occasionally, but not where most people should be living most of the time.

The beauty of RPE is that it accounts for everything going on in your body on a given day. We don’t always feel the same. Sleep, stress, nutrition, and how recently you trained all affect how hard a given weight feels. RPE lets you auto-regulate on a day when everything feels heavier than usual; an RPE of 8 might look different than it does on a great day, and that’s okay. The scale travels with you.

It takes a little practice to calibrate and most people tend to underestimate their RPE at first, rating things as harder than they actually are. But over time it becomes a genuinely reliable internal compass for training intensity and allows you to adjust to how your body is feeling on a given day. Bodies are not machines

Putting It All Together

These three tools work best when you use them together. After a set, ask yourself: how many reps did I have left? How did the weight move? What was my RPE? Over time you’ll start to build an intuitive sense of what “heavy enough” actually feels like for you.

The goal isn’t to go as heavy as possible all the time. The goal is to train at an intensity that’s challenging enough to drive progress, sustainable enough to repeat week after week, and safe enough to keep you in the gym for the long haul.

SSP has six strength training locations across Seattle — Queen Anne, Phinney Ridge, West Seattle, Ballard, Mercer Island, and Wedgwood. If you’re curious about what training with a coach looks like, we offer a free introductory assessment to get you started. Learn more at seattlesp.com.

item.title: Learn to Communicate with more Empathy
item.dc:creator: Chris Maykut
item.description: Two Nonviolent Communication Workshops coming to PhinneyWood Photo by Dwayne joe on Unsplash How do you navigate a difficult conversation without falling into blame, defensiveness, or misunderstanding? And how can […]
item.content:encoded:
Two Nonviolent Communication Workshops coming to PhinneyWood

Photo by Dwayne joe on Unsplash

How do you navigate a difficult conversation without falling into blame, defensiveness, or misunderstanding? And how can you express what you actually need while still making room to hear the person on the other side?

A Center for Restorative Solutions Seattle is offering two upcoming in-person workshops exploring those questions through Nonviolent Communication (NVC), an approach to communication centered around empathy, honesty, self-awareness, and connection. Led by facilitator Pam Orbach, the workshops offer two different entry points: a two-day introduction for people who are new to NVC, followed the next weekend by a deeper dive for those who already have some familiarity with the practice.

Whether you’re interested in communicating differently with a partner or family member, navigating challenging workplace conversations, working within community organizations, or simply becoming more aware of your own patterns when conflict arises, the two workshops offer an opportunity to slow those interactions down and practice another approach.

Learn more about the Level 1 workshop on the PhinneyWood Community Calendar or through A Center for Restorative Solutions Seattle.

Level 1: An Introduction to Compassionate Communication

Saturday & Sunday, September 26–27 | 9 a.m.–4 p.m. | Greenwood

The two-day Compassionate Communication Level 1 workshop introduces participants to the foundations of Nonviolent Communication and its role in restorative practice. Designed for anyone interested in developing greater self-connection and more meaningful engagement with others, the workshop will combine teaching and practice around skills for communicating with greater honesty and empathy.

Participants will explore foundational NVC concepts such as separating observable facts from interpretations, recognizing the assumptions that can fuel conflict, and developing practices intended to reduce blame and shame while creating more opportunities for genuine connection.

No previous NVC experience is necessary. The workshop takes place in person in Greenwood, with the specific address shared upon registration.

Level 2: Deepening NVC

Saturday, October 3 | 9 a.m.–4 p.m. | North Seattle

For those who already know the basics, NVC Level 2: Deepening NVC offers a full day to strengthen those skills and explore how they work in more complex situations. Also led by Pam Orbach, the follow-on workshop uses a combination of teaching, experiential exercises, and community practice to revisit and expand upon foundational NVC skills.

Participants will also look beyond individual conversations to consider how NVC principles intersect with the ways we frame the world and the power structures that shape our experiences—and how greater awareness of those forces can create more choice and intention in the ways we engage with others.

Level 2 is designed as a continuation for people who have completed an introductory NVC training, although anyone with a basic understanding of the model is welcome. The workshop has a $200 value, with sliding-scale rates available.

Questions about either workshop can be directed to Pam.Orbach@EmpoweringConnection.com.

item.title: Meet PhinneyWood’s new pelvic health practice at Spring Physical Therapy’s open house
item.dc:creator: Chris Maykut
item.content:encoded:
A new health and wellness practice has joined the neighborhood! Spring Physical Therapy recently opened its new clinic at 7216 Linden Ave N, specializing in pelvic floor physical therapy with a particular focus on supporting women during pregnancy, postpartum recovery, and beyond.

Spring works with patients on everything from pelvic and low-back pain, to core and pelvic floor strength, incontinence, diastasis recti, birth preparation, and returning comfortably and confidently to exercise and everyday activities. The practice also works collaboratively with doulas, midwives, OBs, and other members of a patient’s care team.

Now, they’re inviting both neighbors and fellow providers to come see the new space and meet the people behind the practice.

On Wednesday, September 23, from 5–8 p.m., they will host a community Open House designed to be both a welcoming introduction for families and an opportunity for local health and wellness professionals to connect and network.

Curious about pelvic floor physical therapy or wondering whether it might be helpful for you? Come by, explore the clinic, meet the team, and ask questions. Local providers are also encouraged to stop in, learn more about Spring’s services, and make connections with others working with families in our community.

And this is very much a family-friendly affair. Throughout the evening there will be snacks and refreshments, activities for kids, permanent jewelry, and raffles, so feel free to bring the whole crew.

Spring Physical Therapy Open House
Wednesday, September 23
5–8 p.m.
7216 Linden Ave N
Kids welcome!

RSVP for the Open House

And welcome to the neighborhood, Spring Physical Therapy!

item.title: Gumshoe 2026 raises a record $11,677—and they’re looking for a Few Good Sleuths for 2027
item.dc:creator: Chris Maykut
item.description: The clues have been solved, the forms have been turned in, and those slightly squished banners atop Red Mill are finally coming down. (Apparently, the Gumshoe Answer Man has not […]
item.content:encoded:
The clues have been solved, the forms have been turned in, and those slightly squished banners atop Red Mill are finally coming down. (Apparently, the Gumshoe Answer Man has not allowed anyone to forget their less-than-perfect installation.) That can mean only one thing: the 2026 Gumshoe is officially in the books, and it was a very good year.

$11,677 for Ballard Food Bank and Aurora Commons

This year’s Gumshoe raised and donated $11,677 to Ballard Food Bank and Aurora Commons—a whopping 33% increase over last year’s $8,773. As the Gumshoe team put it, “We don’t want to get too far into our own spreadsheet feelings about that, but it’s a good number.” Whether participants solved every clue, found themselves hopelessly stumped somewhere around Clue #19, or bought an entry form with every intention of participating and somehow never quite got around to it, it all counted. Even better, the 2026 contribution brings the Gumshoe’s cumulative fundraising to more than $125,000 since 2006.

Not bad for a neighborhood walk!

A Big Thank You to 15 Neighborhood Businesses

The Gumshoe wouldn’t happen without local businesses willing to get in on the fun, and this year 15 neighborhood businesses donated prizes for the people spending their summer wandering PhinneyWood looking suspiciously closely at buildings, signs, alleys, and other neighborhood oddities. A huge thank you goes to El Chupacabra, Pete’s Eggnest, PCC Greenlake, Halcyon, Chicken Supply, Take 5 Urban Market, Ridge Pizza, Nutty Squirrel, Cheeky & Dry, Kym’s Kiddy Corner, Greenwood Hardware, Chez Phinney, Red Mill Burgers, Phinney Books, and Gorgeous George’s.

The Gumshoe team’s suggestion for thanking them? Go spend some actual money at these businesses. “Not as a guilt trip,” they clarified. “Okay, a little as a guilt trip.”

More Than a Walking Quiz

For anyone new to the neighborhood, the annual Gumshoe is part scavenger hunt, part walking tour, part fundraiser, and part elaborate excuse to make people pay closer attention to the place they call home. Participants might find themselves studying a hand-painted fire hydrant, discovering a shortcut through an alley, or finally noticing a shop they’ve walked past hundreds of times without ever stepping inside. And yes, sometimes solving a clue apparently requires finding a mug hidden in a Ridwell bin.

The whole wonderfully quirky tradition even caught the attention of The Seattle Times this year, which featured the Gumshoe as one of three Seattle neighborhood traditions helping build community connections. As the Gumshoe team observed, it took a professional journalist to confirm that “a homemade walking quiz about alleys and hand-painted signs is, in fact, a real thing that brings a neighborhood together.” Around here, we already knew that.

Want to Help Make Gumshoe 2027 Happen?

Here’s where you come in. The Gumshoe may look effortless when you’re strolling around the neighborhood puzzling over clues, but putting it together each summer takes a crew of volunteers—and the team is actively looking for more people to help in 2027. This isn’t a request for a second job or a summer-long commitment. They’re looking for neighbors who can lend a few hours here and there with things like selling entry forms outside Greenwood Hardware, test-walking the route before it goes public, and hanging posters and yard signs around the neighborhood.

The test-walkers have a particularly important job: making sure a tree hasn’t been trimmed, a sign hasn’t disappeared, or some other neighborhood change hasn’t rendered an otherwise brilliant clue completely nonsensical before hundreds of Gumshoes encounter it. If spending a few hours next summer helping perpetuate one of PhinneyWood’s strangest and most beloved traditions sounds like fun, reach out to the Gumshoe team at contact@dothegumshoe.org.

Congratulations to everyone who walked, solved, donated, sponsored, volunteered—and eventually came back to collect their free mug.

item.title: Art Meets Theatre: “Reflections on Conscience” Comes to Taproot’s Greenwood Gallery
item.dc:creator: Chris Maykut
item.description: When the curtain rises on Conscience at Taproot Theatre this month, the story won’t be confined to the stage. Throughout the run of Taproot’s latest production, the theatre’s lobby gallery will feature Reflections on […]
item.content:encoded:
When the curtain rises on Conscience at Taproot Theatre this month, the story won’t be confined to the stage.

Throughout the run of Taproot’s latest production, the theatre’s lobby gallery will feature Reflections on Conscience, a solo exhibition by artist Liesl Lavery inspired by the same remarkable historical figure at the center of the play: U.S. Senator Margaret Chase Smith. It makes for an intriguing intersection of visual art, theatre, and history.

Taproot’s Conscience, by playwright Joe DiPietro, tells the true story of Margaret Chase Smith, the Republican senator from Maine who took to the Senate floor in 1950 to deliver what became known as her Declaration of Conscience. At a time when Senator Joseph McCarthy’s accusations of Communist infiltration of the State Department and scare tactics against fellow politicians and government officials were fueling fear across the country, Smith publicly rejected the political climate of character assassination and fear, taking a stand that put her at odds with members of her own party.

Taproot describes the regional premiere as the story of one person “summoning the courage to speak the truth”—and the personal cost that followed. For Lavery, that same story became the starting point for an entirely different body of work:

Transcribing Margaret Chase Smith’s Declaration of Conscience word for word in watercolor and ink, rooted me in her courage and opened the door to creating an original series inspired by her truth. She was a light in dark times— and relevant as ever.

Lavery’s Reflections on Conscience series combines bold linocut prints, hand-drawn typography, and collage to explore integrity, civic courage, political extremism, and what it means to speak up when doing so comes with consequences. Her use of vibrant color, sharp visual contrasts, text, and imagery invites viewers to consider their own relationship with conscience and courage.

That means a trip to Taproot during the production offers two opportunities to encounter the same questions: first through the artwork surrounding audiences in the lobby, and then through the actors bringing Smith’s story to life onstage.

Reflections on Conscience will be on display in Taproot’s lobby gallery from September 18 – October 17, coinciding with the run of Conscience on the Jewell Mainstage. The play itself runs September 16 – October 17 at Taproot Theatre, 204 N 85th Street, right in the heart of Greenwood. For those looking for an affordable opportunity to see the production, Taproot will offer a Pay What You Can performance on Wednesday, September 23 at 7:30 p.m.

And the next time you head to Taproot, give yourself a little extra time before the curtain—or linger afterward. There’s more than one show worth seeing.

item.title: PhinneyWood original A la Mode Pies holding a pop-up at Flying Bike
item.dc:creator: Chris Maykut
item.description: A la Mode Pies is coming home to PhinneyWood! After more than a decade in the neighborhood, the beloved pie shop said goodbye to its longtime location at 59th and […]
item.content:encoded:
A la Mode Pies is coming home to PhinneyWood! After more than a decade in the neighborhood, the beloved pie shop said goodbye to its longtime location at 59th and Phinney when the property was redeveloped into permanently affordable housing. Now, A la Mode is preparing to return just steps from its former home, with a new location on the ground floor of the Woodland View Apartments.

While we wait for the doors to open, there’s a delicious way to help support their move back to the neighborhood: order a pie, and perhaps have a tasty pint while you’re at it.

A La Mode is officially coming back to the corner that owns our hearts: targeting a late 2026 reopening of our flagship location in Phinney Ridge!

Luckily, you don’t have to wait long for a first taste: with renovations underway, your support is more important than ever. We’re popping up with whole pies at Flying Bike Brewery (8570 Greenwood Ave N) on Saturday September 19 from 5-7 PM! Enjoy fan-favorite French apple, juicy summer peach, brand new Wildberry, and more!

Order your pies now at the link in our bio, or online at alamodeseattle.com – always double check time and location when placing an order. See you soon, Phinney!”
